# {{project.name}}

> A small reactive HTML templating system for browser interfaces built with JavaScript template literals, functions, state, effects, and web standards.

Package: `{{project.name}}`
Version: `{{project.version}}`
Documentation: https://markup.beforesemicolon.com/documentation/
Complete context: https://markup.beforesemicolon.com/llms-full.txt

Markup does not require JSX, a virtual DOM, or a build step. Its three primary APIs are `html`, `state`, and `effect`. Use the installed package version and these documents as authoritative; do not substitute React, Lit, Vue, or browser APIs that are not documented here.

## Package boundaries

- `@beforesemicolon/markup`: reactive templates, state, effects, and template helpers.
- `@beforesemicolon/web-component`: Custom Elements, props, component state, lifecycle callbacks, events, slots, parts, refs, styles, and form-associated controls.
- `@beforesemicolon/router`: route matching, navigation, page data, redirects, query state, and route-aware rendering.
- `@beforesemicolon/intl`: locale scopes, translated messages, and internationalized formatting.

Read the companion package documentation before generating code that uses its APIs:

- https://web-component.beforesemicolon.com/
- https://router.beforesemicolon.com/
- https://intl.beforesemicolon.com/

The ecosystem dependency direction is:

1. Markup is the rendering and reactivity foundation.
2. Web Component depends on and re-exports Markup.
3. Router and Intl depend on Web Component and may be installed together.

Choose imports by ownership:

- In a Markup-only application, import rendering APIs from `@beforesemicolon/markup`.
- In a Web Component application, import Markup APIs from `@beforesemicolon/web-component`; it already re-exports them.
- Import navigation APIs and register route elements through `@beforesemicolon/router`.
- Import locale runtimes, formatters, and register Intl elements through `@beforesemicolon/intl`.
- Router and Intl do not re-export `html` or `WebComponent`.

For direct browser scripts, load Web Component before Router or Intl. Router and Intl can then be loaded in either order.

## Installation and imports

ES modules:

```javascript
import {
    html,
    state,
    effect,
    when,
    repeat,
    pick,
    is,
    isNot,
    and,
    or,
    oneOf,
    element,
    suspense,
    visible,
    unsafeHTML,
} from '@beforesemicolon/markup'
```

Direct browser usage:

```html
<script src="https://unpkg.com/@beforesemicolon/markup/dist/client.js"></script>
<script>
    const { html, state, effect, when, repeat } = BFS.MARKUP
</script>
```

The CDN build exposes the API as `BFS.MARKUP`. npm imports use named exports.

## Core mental model

1. `html` creates an `HtmlTemplate` from an HTML tagged template literal.
2. Functions interpolated into a template are evaluated lazily.
3. Calling a state getter while a template binding or effect is running records that dependency.
4. Updating the state schedules only the dependent template bindings and effects.
5. State values change immediately; reactive DOM work and subscribers are batched in a microtask.
6. Template updates run before user effects responding to the same state change.

Markup templates contain HTML, not JSX. Use `class`, `for`, `onclick`, and other HTML attribute names rather than React-specific names such as `className`, `htmlFor`, or `onClick`.

## `html`

```typescript
html(parts: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]): HtmlTemplate
```

Create and render a template:

```javascript
const greeting = html`<h1>Hello</h1>`
greeting.render(document.getElementById('app'))
```

Interpolations accept primitives, functions, DOM nodes, nested `HtmlTemplate` instances, and one-dimensional arrays containing renderable values.

Reactive and one-time values are intentionally different:

```javascript
const [count, setCount] = state(0)

html`${count}`   // reactive: Markup calls the getter and tracks it
html`${count()}` // one-time value: evaluates before the template is created

const doubled = () => count() * 2
html`<p>${doubled}</p>` // reactive derived value
```

Pass getters and derived functions directly when a value must remain reactive. Call them before interpolation only when a snapshot is intentional.

Reactive attributes follow the same rule:

```javascript
const [disabled, setDisabled] = state(false)
const [theme, setTheme] = state('light')

const button = html`
    <button disabled="${disabled}" class="button ${theme}">Save</button>
`
```

Do not interpolate dynamic tag names into an `html` template. Use the `element` helper for dynamic element names.

Interpolated strings are rendered as values and are not parsed as HTML. Keep
untrusted and runtime-provided content in interpolations:

```javascript
const message = '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'
html`<p>${message}</p>` // rendered as text, not as an img element
```

Use `unsafeHTML(source)` only when deliberately parsing trusted or independently
sanitized markup. Never pass user-controlled content to it. Passing manually
constructed string arrays to `html`, such as `html([source])`, is retained only
for backward compatibility and is deprecated in favor of `unsafeHTML(source)`.

## `state`

```typescript
state<T>(
    initialValue: T,
    subscriber?: () => void
): readonly [
    getValue: () => T,
    setValue: (next: T | ((previous: T) => T)) => T,
    unsubscribeSubscriber: () => void,
]
```

```javascript
const [count, setCount] = state(0)

setCount(1)
console.log(count()) // 1 immediately

setCount((previous) => previous + 1)
```

State uses `Object.is` to detect changes. Do not mutate an object or array and set the same reference. Return a new value:

```javascript
setTodos((previous) => [
    ...previous,
    { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name: 'New todo' },
])
```

State is independent of templates and components, so it may live in a module and act as a shared store.

## `effect`

```typescript
effect<T>(
    callback: (previousResult: T | undefined) => T | undefined
): () => void
```

An effect runs immediately, tracks state getters called during that run, and reruns after those states change. Dependencies are collected again on every run.

```javascript
const [query, setQuery] = state('')

const stop = effect(() => {
    console.log('Current query:', query())
})

setQuery('markup')
stop()
```

The value returned by the callback is cached and passed as `previousResult` on the next execution. It is not an effect cleanup function. The function returned by `effect` unsubscribes and disposes the effect.

```javascript
effect((timer) => {
    clearTimeout(timer)
    const value = query()

    return setTimeout(() => search(value), 250)
})
```

Use effects for side effects. Put rendered derived values directly in templates as functions.

The initial effect execution follows normal JavaScript order. Refs do not exist before rendering. After a template is rendered, state-driven template updates and refs are committed before responding user effects run:

```javascript
const [open, setOpen] = state(false)
const form = html`<form ref="form"><input /></form>`
const view = html`${when(open, form, '')}`.render(document.body)

effect(() => {
    if (!open()) return
    const [formElement] = view.refs.form ?? []
    formElement?.querySelector('input')?.focus()
})
```

## Events

Event attributes receive functions and are installed with `addEventListener`. The event attribute is not emitted into the resulting HTML.

```javascript
const save = (event) => {
    event.preventDefault()
}

html`<form onsubmit="${save}"></form>`
```

Pass listener options as `[handler, options]`:

```javascript
html`<button onclick="${[handleClick, { once: true }]}">Run once</button>`
```

Do not call the handler during template creation:

```javascript
html`<button onclick="${handleClick}">Correct</button>`
```

## Conditional rendering with `when`

```typescript
when(condition, thenValue, elseValue?): () => unknown
```

Use `when` when the condition is reactive:

```javascript
const [loading, setLoading] = state(false)

const content = html`
    ${when(
        loading,
        html`<p>Loading...</p>`,
        html`<button>Load</button>`
    )}
`
```

Inactive template branches are unmounted. Their refs are not included until the branch is mounted.

## Reactive collections with `repeat`

```typescript
repeat(data, renderItem, emptyTemplateOrOptions?): () => unknown
```

Use `repeat` instead of `.map()` for collections that change:

```javascript
const [todos, setTodos] = state([])

const list = html`
    <ul>
        ${repeat(
            todos,
            (todo) => html`<li>${todo.name}</li>`,
            {
                key: (todo) => todo.id,
                empty: () => html`<li>No todos</li>`,
            }
        )}
    </ul>
`
```

Prefer an explicit stable key. Without one, Markup uses an object's non-null `id` property when available and otherwise uses the item value or identity. Duplicate explicit or object `id` keys throw an error. Stable keys and stable item references allow rendered item templates to be reused; replacing an item object allows that item template to be recreated or rebound.

`repeat` also accepts numbers, strings, Sets, Maps, object entries, and custom iterables. Use plain `.map()` only for a static collection rendered once.

## Refs

```javascript
const view = html`
    <h1 ref="heading">Title</h1>
    <button ref="action">Save</button>
`.render(document.body)

const [heading] = view.refs.heading
```

`refs` is a record of arrays because multiple elements may share a name. A parent template aggregates refs from currently mounted nested templates. The record is dynamic: unmounted branches disappear and newly mounted branches appear. Always handle a missing ref.

## Template lifecycle and placement

An `HtmlTemplate` supports:

- `render(target)` to mount it or move an already mounted template.
- `replace(nodeOrTemplate)` to replace a node or another template.
- `insertAfter(nodeOrTemplate)` to insert or move after a target.
- `unmount()` to remove it and dispose its reactive bindings.
- `onMount(callback)`; the callback may return an unmount cleanup function.
- `onUpdate(callback)` after a reactive template binding changes.
- `onMove(callback)` after an already mounted template moves.
- `toString()` to serialize its current content.
- `refs`, `childNodes`, `parentNode`, and `mounted` for current template state.

Lifecycle and placement methods return the template and may be chained:

```javascript
const view = html`<p>${message}</p>`
    .onMount(() => {
        const controller = new AbortController()
        startWork(controller.signal)
        return () => controller.abort()
    })
    .onUpdate((template) => console.log(template.toString()))
    .render(document.body)
```

## Other helpers

- `pick(valueOrGetter, 'nested.path', mapper?)`: creates a reactive deep-property getter.
- `is(valueOrGetter, expectedOrPredicate?)`: creates a reactive equality, predicate, regular-expression, or truthiness check.
- `isNot(...)`: negated `is` check.
- `and(...conditions)`: reactive truthiness conjunction; requires at least two inputs.
- `or(...conditions)`: reactive truthiness disjunction; requires at least two inputs.
- `oneOf(valueOrGetter, values)`: reactive membership check.
- `suspense(asyncAction, loadingTemplate?, errorTemplate?)`: renders loading content and replaces it after the promise settles.
- `visible(content, placeholder?, options?)`: renders content when it intersects the viewport; `eager: true` renders immediately.
- `element(tagName, options?)`: creates a DOM element programmatically for dynamic tag names and attributes.
- `val(valueOrGetter)`: unwraps a value or function, mainly when implementing helpers.

Read the helper's documentation before using advanced arguments or relying on lifecycle behavior.

## Complete application pattern

```javascript
import { html, state, effect, when, repeat } from '@beforesemicolon/markup'

const [todos, setTodos] = state([])
const [draft, setDraft] = state('')

const addTodo = (event) => {
    event.preventDefault()
    const name = draft().trim()
    if (!name) return

    setTodos((previous) => [
        ...previous,
        { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name },
    ])
    setDraft('')
}

const removeTodo = (id) => {
    setTodos((previous) => previous.filter((todo) => todo.id !== id))
}

const renderTodo = (todo) => html`
    <li>
        <span>${todo.name}</span>
        <button type="button" onclick="${() => removeTodo(todo.id)}">
            Delete
        </button>
    </li>
`

const app = html`
    <form onsubmit="${addTodo}">
        <input
            ref="draft"
            value="${draft}"
            oninput="${(event) => setDraft(event.target.value)}"
        />
        <button type="submit">Add todo</button>
    </form>

    ${when(
        () => todos().length > 0,
        html`<ul>${repeat(todos, renderTodo, { key: (todo) => todo.id })}</ul>`,
        html`<p>No todos yet.</p>`
    )}
`

app.render(document.getElementById('app'))

effect(() => {
    todos()
    const [input] = app.refs.draft ?? []
    input?.focus()
})
```

## Rules for generated code

- Use normal HTML attribute names, not JSX names.
- Pass state getters or derived functions directly for reactive bindings.
- Do not call getters in a template unless a one-time snapshot is intended.
- Use immutable state updates so `Object.is` detects a new value.
- Use `when` for reactive branches and `repeat` for reactive lists.
- Prefer stable explicit keys for application collections.
- Keep side effects in `effect` or lifecycle callbacks.
- Render a template before expecting its refs to exist.
- Treat refs as dynamic arrays of currently mounted elements.
- Return cleanup from `onMount`; call the function returned by `effect` to dispose an effect.
- Do not return a React-style cleanup function from an effect callback; its return value is cached data.
- Do not add React Hooks, JSX, a virtual DOM, or framework-specific component conventions.
- Do not invent Markup APIs. Read the relevant canonical page when uncertain.
